It was likewise so. The nature of worldly phenomena is impermanent; he then expounded upon the Dharma of the four foundations of mindfulness in detail. Upon hearing this, Emperor [Liang Wu] was startled into awakening and broke into a sweat.

Consequently, he received the Bodhisattva precepts, renounced alcohol and meat, released hawks and falcons, and put an end to fishing and hunting. He prohibited slaughter throughout the empire and issued decrees six times a month, three times a year, commanding the people to observe the fast and maintain discipline.

Donggong Tang Xuawan was a native of Huayin in Hongnong. At the beginning of the Zhenguan era, the Emperor—recognizing that Xuawan’s moral integrity and virtue were held in high esteem by both the court and the commonalty—issued an edict appointing him to bestow the Bodhisattva precepts upon the Crown Prince and the various princes.
Xuawan sent a letter to the Crown Prince, stating: "Now, briefly..."

There are four essential points in the scriptures; I pray that you will pay close attention to them. The first is the practice of compassion (*maitrī*). This means nourishing and providing universal relief in accordance with the texts on the Brahma-conduct (*brahmacarya*) of *nirvāṇa*.
The second is the reduction of slaughter. This refers to the fact that the regular meals of the Eastern Palace involve the slaughtering of many animals.

Your Highness uses the provisions for one person’s portion to serve the entire body of officials, yet when it comes to the actual taking of life, no one takes responsibility for the source of these provisions.
Your Highness, please reduce the taking of life to prolong your lifespan. Third is "Harmonizing the Qi": this means that non-killing is called benevolence (*ren*).

Benevolence presides over the liver and wood; wood belongs to the spring season of growth. Your Highness occupies the position of Minor Yang; I pray that you prohibit killing and abstain from meat during the spring months.
To accord with the harmony of Yang (the principle of growth). Fourth is the observance of the fast (*zhāi*). This refers to the three annual fasts and the six monthly fasts. Why is this?

Our present enjoyment of great fortune is entirely dependent on past causes; furthermore, being able to advance in virtue makes it even more excellent. The Crown Prince replied: "I am honored by the Master’s four categories of sublime Dharma.
I shall reverently seal them within the treasury of my heart and uphold them in all my conduct, forever relying upon these superior causes to support [my practice]."
Through the profound protection of the unseen, [the Emperor] exhorted him to cease slaughter.

The Tang dynasty śramaṇa Mingzhan was by nature a man of broad learning and harbored ambitions for statecraft. When Taizong heard of his reputation, he issued an imperial decree summoning him into the palace.

The Emperor questioned him, and Sengzhan extensively expounded upon the essentials of governance. He further explained that the Buddhist tradition takes compassionate salvation as its fundamental principle.

Emperor Taizong was greatly pleased and issued an edict decreeing that during the three months of spring and the six days of fasting each month, the slaughter of animals shall be universally prohibited, and temples shall be established at all military encampments.
Exhortation to Practice the Dharma of Repentance (Liu).
Tánzōng of the Song dynasty was a native of Mólíng. He entered the monastic order at Língwèi Temple. He once performed the Bodhisattva’s Fivefold Repentance for Emperor Wŭdi.
The Emperor laughed and said to Zōng, "What sins do I have that you should perform repentance on my behalf? Zōng replied, "In the past, Yúshùn..."
Even the Most Sage [Shun] said, "If I err, you must assist me. Tang and Wu also said, "If the myriad people commit transgressions, the fault lies with me alone.
That sage-kings took the blame upon themselves was precisely to guide the world. Your Majesty’s sagely virtue equals that of antiquity; you tread the Way with humble reflection.
How could you possibly be an exception? Emperor Wu praised this.

Shoufa Buqi (Virtue of Not Deceiving Others), courtesy name Daokai, was a native of Yishui. After attaining the Dharma, he greatly propagated the tradition of Dongshan. During the Chongning era, an imperial decree appointed him as abbot of Jingyin Monastery in the Eastern Capital;
during the Daguan era, he was transferred to Tianning Monastery. The Emperor dispatched an envoy to bestow upon him purple robes and the title Chan Master Dingzhao.
The Master declined the offer, declining to accept it. The Emperor again ordered Li Xiaoshou, the Governor of Kaifeng, to personally convey the court’s intention to praise his virtuous conduct.
Yet Huikai remained firm and would not change his mind. The Emperor grew angry and had him arrested and handed over to the authorities.
When the officials learned of Huikai’s loyalty and integrity, they asked him, "Elder, are you emaciated and ill? He replied, "I am not ill. The officials said, "If you say you are ill—"

He was immediately exempted from punishment. Huikai said, "How could I dare feign illness to seek exemption from guilt and censure? The officials sighed in admiration; he then accepted the penalty and was sent to be registered in Zizhou.
Those who saw him shed tears, yet Huikai’s countenance remained composed. Upon arriving at the prefecture, he rented a house to live in, and his students drew closer to him than ever.
The following year, by imperial decree, he was released to live as he pleased, whereupon he built a hermitage on Fuyong Lake.

The commentary states: To receive an honor and yet decline it is difficult for people to do; to decline it and thereby incur punishment, yet to accept that punishment without deception—is this not the "difficult within the difficult"?
How could such a person be lacking in the Biographies of the Loyal and Virtuous? I have recorded this to serve as an exhortation for the monastics of the world.
On "Praising Flowers as a Satirical Admonition":
Later, during the Southern Tang period of the Later Jin, Li Houzhu summoned Chan Master Fayan to the inner court. At that time, peonies were in full bloom.

The Lord requested a poem, and the Master offered this verse: *Clad in coarse wool, facing a fragrant thicket,* *From the start, we have always been far apart.* *The hair [of my head] follows from now on...*
The sun rises and speaks: "These flowers were red last year; their brilliance now differs as they follow the morning dew, and their fragrance drifts with the evening breeze.
Why wait for them to wither and fall before one finally realizes their emptiness? The host sighed, having awakened to the meaning of the verse.
The commentary states: "Tasting the meaning of this poem, one’s loyal affection overflows naturally from its words. It is a pity that the late ruler knew of it yet did not employ it;
in the end, he could not avoid the regret of indulging in pleasure within a dream.

As for those called 'poet-monks,' they spend their essence on critiquing the wind and moon and laboriously refining their推敲 (qiāo) verses, yet these offer no benefit to the world. Compared to this [poem], are they not as different as gold and soil?"
Are they far apart?
○ General Discussion:
When a scholar-official dwells far away from the capital, he worries for his sovereign. A monk has no official duties to guard; a monk has no words [of remonstrance].
This is indeed a matter of reprimand. Yet, one can be so utterly loyal; who would say that beneath the mountain forests there is no principle of the "enlightened and virtuous rising in joy"?
Among human relations, none are more important than those toward sovereign and father. Therefore, I have placed the monk’s filiality first and his loyalty last.
This is to refute the slander of the Śākyas for having neither father nor sovereign.
△ Sixth: The Practice of Compassion Toward Beings—Enduring Suffering to Protect the Geese.
In the time of the Buddha, there was a bhikṣu who went to the door of a pearl-worker to beg for alms. At that time, the pearl-worker was fashioning pearls for the king;

he had set aside some pearls to take with him for his meal, but they happened to fall to the ground and were swallowed by a goose. When the pearl-worker gave food to the bhikṣu, he looked for the pearls but could not see them.
Suspecting that the bhikṣu had stolen them, the worker beat the bhikṣu until he bled, all the while the bhikṣu, wishing to protect the goose, remained silent and endured the blows.
There was blood. A goose came to lick the blood. The jeweler, shifting his anger, struck the goose and killed it. The bhikṣu could not help but weep with grief.
The jeweler marveled at this and spoke to him; thus, he attained realization. The jeweler repented and prostrated before him.

Huyue Jinyin (Huyue Jinyin) was a Jin dynasty monk who maintained a life of purity and poverty while observing strict ascetic discipline. He built a hermitage on Mount Huo in Lujiang County; the mountain is situated in the midst of the sea.

There is a stone basin there several *zhang* in diameter, filled with clear, bracing spring water. The hermitage is separated from the stone by a small stream, crossed by a bridge made of a single tree trunk. Proceeding [from the bridge],...

While drawing water, one of the ducks later broke its wing and remained on the bridge. The group wished to lift their alms-bowls to nudge it away, but fearing they might injure the duck, they did not go back to draw water.
They went without drinking until they passed away.
The Eulogy says: To forget one’s own body for the sake of the lives of other beings—such is the ultimate extent of great compassion and universal salvation. Someone might say:
"It is acceptable to spare the goose at the cost of enduring suffering, but is it not a transgression to extinguish the lives of the entire flock?
Alas! To the Perfect Man, this skin-sack is but a dream, an illusion, a bubble, or a shadow. If there is benefit for sentient beings, he would discard it like mucus or spittle. To feed [the flock]...
The tiger feeding the hawk does so with this very same mind; how could it be fathomed by ordinary people who cling greedily to the four great elements?
Chen Falang, a native of Paixian County in Xuzhou, studied Chan under Master Baizhi of Daming Temple and was refined in the Vinaya. He ransomed and nurtured living beings.

The treatise states: His reputation spread throughout the capital region, and disciples gathered like clouds. The alms he received were used to produce scriptures, images, stupas, and monasteries, and to provide relief to the poor and distressed.
Whenever he saw living beings, he would purchase them to keep as his livestock; geese, ducks, chickens, and dogs filled his quarters.

He saw Lang sleeping in tranquility, entirely silent. Yet, when he had previously visited and observed him, the dogs would all rise together to bark and howl, clamoring like the sound of drums and pipes.
Was this perhaps due to the depth of his spiritual resonance? Moved by both sorrow and reverence, he practiced the giving of alms.
Sui Lingyu was a native of Julu in Dingzhou. At the age of fifteen, he entered the monastic order at Yingjue Monastery in Zhaojun.
He was widely learned in the sūtras and śāstras, and his reputation spread throughout the realm. In his practice of giving, he combined both compassion and reverence;

he bestowed more than a thousand monastic robes and provided immeasurable medicine for those seeking treatment for their illnesses. Whenever he obtained rich flavors, he would invariably offer them first to the Sangha, even when... [text truncated]

He never once scolded or spat upon domestic animals; even when reprimanding children or instructing his disciples, he addressed them by their own names while referring to himself as "that benevolent one.
His words were so bitter and earnest that those who heard them would shed tears.
Regarding the purchase of a pond for releasing captive life by the Great Master Zhizhe of the Sui Dynasty:

While he was residing in Linhai, he saw that the local people made their living as fishermen, with fishing nets extending for over four hundred li and more than sixty dams and bridges spanning the rivers, streams, and canals. Moved by compassion, he took the offerings he had received and used them [to purchase the land].
He purchased land by the seaside to establish it as a *fangsheng chi* (a pond for the release of living beings) and submitted a memorial to inform the Chen Emperor.

The Emperor issued an edict prohibiting the catching of aquatic life and subsequently erected a stele for the site. He commissioned Xu Xiaoké, the Director of the National University, to compose the inscription; the wording was profoundly poignant, moving readers to sorrowful realization.
There were many who were moved by his transformation.
Zhi Shun of the Sui dynasty was a native of Zhaozhou. While traveling north to a hermitage on Mount Ting, he encountered a hunter pursuing a pheasant that had entered [the mountain].

Shun’s wife [was captured]. Shun earnestly exhorted her to release her, but she would not listen; consequently, he cut off his own ears and gave them to her. The hunter was startled into realization; he cast away his bow and released his hawk.

Several villages abandoned their hunting livelihoods. Whenever he saw those who were impoverished and starving, tears filled his face; he stripped off his clothes and reduced his own food, going to such lengths as these.
The commentary says: Mencius said, "There has never been one who was perfectly sincere yet failed to move others. This was verified in the case of Shun in his old age.
As for Jìpín Yìguān (Ji Pu’an), he was a native of Jīngzhào Jīngyáng. When the Zhou dynasty suppressed the Dharma, he lived in seclusion among the *pián* and *zǐ* trees on Mount Zhōngnán.

In the valleys, [Hui]an practiced asceticism to the point of forgetting his own body. At times he exposed himself among the weeds and brush to offer his flesh to mosquitoes and gadflies; at other times he lay down amidst scattered corpses to offer himself to tigers and leopards.
At that time, there was a heavy bounty offered: anyone who captured and delivered a monk would be rewarded with ten rolls of silk.

When someone came to seize him, An greeted them with joy and comforted them, saying, "I see you are suffering from poverty and I wish to provide for you. After he had prepared food for them, he entered [the city] with them.
The Emperor said, "In my country's laws, it is strictly forbidden to allow monks among the common people.
If you further assist in making it strictly forbidden for monks in the mountains as well, then where would you send them? Thereupon, he allowed him to enter the mountains.

Tang Zhiyan was a native of Qu’ea in Danyang who personally resided in a leper ward. His wisdom and courage surpassed those of ordinary men, and he served as a General of the Tiger Guards (*hùbēn zhōnglángjiāng*).
It was his constant practice to hang a filtering cloth from the tip of his bow. Later, he entered Mount Xiàngwàn to rely upon Chan Master Bǎoyuè and left the household life.
Formerly, when the military governor Yan Zuan, Zhang Chuo, and others heard that he had left the household life, they went to seek him out.

Finding him in a secluded and desolate deep mountain, they said to him, "General, have you gone mad? Why are you here? Huayan replied, "My madness desires to awaken, while yours is currently in full bloom.
He then went to the lepers' ward in Shitou City and preached the Dharma for them; there was no one who did not have their pus sucked and their filth washed away.
He exhausted his life in the practice of the Way. During the Yonghui era, he passed away at his dwelling; his countenance did not change, and a rare fragrance lingered for ten days.
Tang Zhikuan was a native of Hedong in Puzhou. He constantly recited the Vimalakīrti Sūtra and the *Prātimokṣa* precepts, which moved the heavenly deities to circumambulate him.

Fang was compassionate and benevolent by nature and delighted in providing for the sick, regardless of whether they were monastics or laypeople, or how far away they lived. Whenever there was no one to treat them, she would immediately have them carried to her room and personally attend to their care.
Once, there was a patient with an abdominal abscess from which the pus could not be drained; she sucked it out with her own mouth.
He subsequently recovered his health. Later, when Xiao Gan plotted a rebellion, Daoxuan was arrested and exiled to Western Sichuan.

He refused all the wealth and silk offered as a farewell gift, carrying only his scriptures on a single donkey. On the road, he encountered the monk Baoxian, whose feet were wounded and who lay by the roadside.
He gave up his donkey and carriage to carry the scriptures himself. When he encountered a year of famine, he would cook gruel to feed the hungry;

he would also take off his own clothes to clothe them, whether by cutting or reducing his own portion. Baring his grief, he exhorted others through his practice of alms-gathering, leading them toward the recitation of the Buddha’s name.
Huìyì of the Tang dynasty nourished a colony of mice.

He would feed the leftovers from his alms bowl to the mice in his room; there were over a hundred that had taken refuge there, all of whom became tame and familiar, vying with one another to come and eat.
When any among them were ill, he would stroke and rub them with his own hands.
Zhanbei Chuxiu and Tang Zhikai.
Zhikai was a native of Danyang who frequently lectured on the *Sanlun* (Three Treatises). In the first year of the Zhenguan era, he resided at Xiaolongquan Temple in Yuyao County.
It was the custom among the people of Yue to abandon puppies on the roads once they were born; Zhikai took pity on them, collected them, and raised them. Thereupon—
By the age of thirty-five or forty, he shared his felt blankets and bedding with others without disliking their filth.

He did not disdain those afflicted by foul diseases, such as Tang Daoji, a man from Shu who resided at Fugan Temple in Yizhou. Daoji was compassionate by nature; there were those suffering from leprosy whose bodies were completely溃烂 (gangrenated).
The foul vapors were so thick and oppressive that those who smelled them would cover their noses. He provided for them with unwavering consistency, his body and mind as one.

At times they ate from the same vessel, and he would occasionally wash and mend their clothes for them. When people questioned him about this, he replied: "Purity and filth are matters of the mind’s aversion and attachment.
How could I allow my spiritual contemplation to be divided? I am merely using this as a means of refinement."

While visiting the sick, he encountered the sage of the Holy Tang dynasty, Zhìhuī, who resided at Chóngyún Monastery. Zhìhuī established a warm bathhouse for monks, providing bathing water and medicine. There was a bhikṣu suffering from leprosy whom the community loathed;
yet Zhìhuī washed and massaged him as usual. Suddenly, there appeared divine light and extraordinary fragrance. Just as the others were marveling at this, the monk vanished.
[The text] records the location.
Zan said: "The Buddha spoke of how, after my parinirvāṇa, one should joyfully make offerings to the sick, for among them there are many worthies and sages.
What Zhongyun has encountered now is precisely similar to the karmic conditions of Wuda. Instances like this are very numerous throughout antiquity and today; let us [consider them] briefly.
He emerged from his seclusion once or twice to exhort those who looked askance at or despised the sick.
His conduct was such that he would always take up the broom first;

Tang Huibin was a man of Yanzhou who had extensively mastered the sutras and treatises, later devoting himself exclusively to meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), making it his primary duty to rescue others through compassion. Every time...
When walking about during the summer, fearing he might harm minute insects, he would first sweep the path with a broom.
Whatever offerings he received, he secretly practiced generosity and performed various kinds of virtuous deeds, strictly admonishing others not to disclose them.
Tánxuǎn of the Táng dynasty, a native of Gāoyáng, resided at Xìngguó Temple. By nature he was fond of compassionate relief; he did not accumulate wealth or goods.

He maintained a large cauldron, into which he poured all the food obtained from alms-seekers to make gruel. He would seat the various beggars in rows and personally distribute the portions with his own hands. Upon seeing them...
His robes were tattered and his body was emaciated; moved by compassion, he wept tears of sorrow, unable to restrain his grief.
He himself also joined the group to receive and eat the gruel, and thus many years passed.

Master Yongming Shouchan of the Five Dynasties practiced giving, upheld the precepts, and released captive animals. During his fifteen years at Yongming, he ordained one thousand seven hundred disciples;

later, at Tiantai, he conferred the full precepts upon over ten thousand people. He constantly bestowed the Bodhisattva precepts upon the seven assemblies of followers and offered food to spirits and deities at night.
He ate sparingly and released various living creatures. He practiced the Way during the six periods of the day; with his remaining strength, he recited the *Lotus Sūtra* thirteen thousand times.
On the twenty-sixth day of the twelfth month of the eighth year of the Kaibao era, he burned incense, addressed the assembly, sat cross-legged, and passed away.

Regarding the care of the sick as if it were one's own, there was Gaofeng Yuanmiao of the Song dynasty. While residing at Yunju, he heard that a monk had fallen ill and been moved to the Yanshou Hall; he sighed with deep compassion as if the illness were his own.

Morning and evening he inquired after the patient’s condition and personally prepared his food and drink. He would not eat until he had tasted what the patient had consumed. When the weather grew slightly cold, he would [comfort the patient].
On their backs, it was written: "Is your clothing not too thin? During the heat, they would examine their complexions and ask: "Are you not suffering from excessive heat?
Even for those who had reached the end of their lives, they did not inquire whether they possessed permanent property or not, but provided them with funeral rites and escorted them away.
The commentary states: The Sūtras speak of eight kinds of fields of merit, and nursing the sick is foremost among them.
Is it not because monastics have no homes, wandering alone across lakes and seas, solitary and afflicted by illness? This is truly a state to be pitied.

If one serves as the abbot of a monastery, yet when a monk falls ill does not provide for his care, and when he dies does not provide for his burial—how can this be called the Way of compassion? Every abbot should follow the example of Gao’an.
This constitutes the Dharma.

○ Generally discussing benevolence, righteousness, propriety, and wisdom: these are the four beginnings of humanity, of which benevolence is the foremost. Compassion, joy, equanimity, and relinquishment: these are the four [immeasurables] of the Buddha.

It is the mind, and compassion (*maitrī*) is its priority. If one lacks a compassionate heart, then even if one possesses extensive learning, vast erudition, supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*), and meditative absorptions (*samādhi*), these are all merely the works of Māra.
Some may say that the simultaneous application of compassion and majestic authority (*vibhūti*) constitutes the Buddha-way;

why then do you exclusively exalt compassion? They fail to realize that giving life and taking it are both acts of benevolence (*ren*); gathering others in and subduing them are both acts of compassion (*ci*). In their outward manifestation they appear as majesty, but in their essence—
This is benevolence (*maitrī*). To be majestic yet not lose one's benevolence—this is called great benevolence (*mahāmaitrī*).
Do not, my son, speak of benevolence in terms of trivial favors or petty kindnesses.
△ Section Seven: Noble Conduct—Avoiding Favor and Entering the Mountains.

Daoheng of the Jin dynasty was coerced by Yao Xing, the ruler of Qin, to change his robes and serve as a counselor. Although he repeatedly declined, his requests were not granted; he narrowly escaped with his life.
He declined. Then he sighed, saying: "An ancient had a saying: 'That which increases my wealth diminishes my spirit; that which gives me fame kills my person.
Thereupon, he vanished his shadow among the crags and gullies, subsisting on herbs while savoring meditation for the rest of his life."
The multitude was moved by their pure and detached demeanor.

During the Jin dynasty, Huiyong and Master Huiyuan resided on Mount Lu. When He Wujī, General Who Pacifies the South, was stationed in Xunyang, he gathered his officers at the Tiger Brook to invite Huiyong and Huiyuan.
Huiyuan’s followers numbered over a hundred; they were dignified and orderly, while Huiyong wore only a patchwork robe and grass matting.
Wearing his sandals, holding his *khakkhara* staff and alms bowl, he arrived with a graceful air beneath the pines. His spirit remained composed and self-possessed.
Huiji said to the assembly, "Master Yong’s style of pure detachment is even more abundant than that of Master Huiyuan."
The commentary states: Master Huiyuan had more than a hundred followers, all of whom were the eminent and virtuous members of the Lotus Society.

Yet, even He Gong (He Chong) could still speak of them with such restraint and praise. Now, there are monks who keep servants, carry parasols and satchels, and scurry to the doors of the wealthy and powerful seeking to associate with them as equals.
When He Gong saw this, how would he have reacted?

He did not accept royal offerings while Fo-tuo-ye-she (Buddhayaśas) was in Guzang during the Yao Qin dynasty. When the Qin ruler Fuxing dispatched an envoy to invite him, he refused the generous gifts.
Upon his arrival, Fuxing personally went out to welcome him and established a new monastic residence for him within the Xiaoyao Garden, providing him with the four requisites of monastic life.
He did not accept them either. When the time came for his almsround, he took but a single meal. Although his robes, bowl, and bedding filled three rooms, he paid them no mind;
he sold them and used the proceeds to build a monastery south of the city.
Emperor Wenxuan never went to welcome or see off the monk Sengchou.
He would often lead his vanguard and guards to the monastery, yet Sengchou remained seated in meditation in his small room and did not go out to greet him at all.
When his disciples remonstrated with him, Sengchou said, "In the past, Piṇḍola welcomed a king for seven paces, which caused the king to lose his kingdom for seven years."
Truly, my virtue falls short of the ideal; I did not dare deceive others regarding my physical appearance, hoping only to obtain blessings from the Emperor.
The world calls me Master Chou, yet I never associated with the nobility or those who frequent the courts.
Liang Zhixin was a native of Danyang. He was renowned throughout the realm for his mastery of the scriptural teachings.

Toward the end of the Yongming era, when the Crown Prince frequently visited various temples during his excursions to the Eastern Garden, Zhixin consequently retired to Mount Zhong on the pretext of illness. There he lived in tranquil self-contentment, no longer associating with those of wealth and status.
Secluded and remote, it was cut off from human habitation. Whenever he received alms, he would not store them, but instead used them to build and renovate the monastery.
It is said that he did not allow bandits to take the path there.

Dao Yue of the Sui dynasty was a native of Jingzhou; he constantly recited the *Prajñāpāramitā* and resided at Yuquan. He encountered the rebellion of Zhu Can, who entered the monastery seeking [him].
Furthermore, they wished to harm him. Yue was not at all afraid; he released them and let them lead the way.
After walking a few paces, Yue sat down on the ground and said, "I am a śramaṇa, not a person to guide the way. This illusory physical form may be left to the mercy of the white blade.
Fan Can was struck by his noble character and consequently escorted him back to the monastery.
Ci-zang of Tang was a man from Silla who practiced in secret yet manifested his virtue openly; he was the object of universal esteem and repeatedly declined imperial summons.

The King became greatly incensed and issued an edict that Zang be sent to his mountain retreat to be executed by the hand of the executioner. Zang said, "I would rather die while observing the precepts for a single day."
He did not wish to be born in a lifetime where he would break the precepts, and thus he could not bear to kill [the animal]. He reported all this to the King, who sighed in admiration.
As for the Fourth Patriarch of the Tang, Master Daoxin, he resided at Huangmei for over thirty years. During the Zhenguan era, Emperor Taizong three times...

An imperial edict ordered him to go to the capital, but he declined on both occasions citing illness. The Emperor commanded a messenger, saying, "If he does not rise [to comply], you shall take his head.

The Master extended his neck to receive the blade. The messenger reported this to the throne. Emperor Taizong sighed in admiration and bestowed precious silks upon him so that he might fulfill his resolve.
The commentary says: Zǐlíng’s refusal of Emperor Guāng and Zhōnglǎo’s resignation from Emperor Rénzǔ were merely the common conduct of reclusive scholars;
yet we have never heard of anyone who, when threatened with a blade of white steel, did not turn back.
Dānfèng soars into the clouds—visible from afar, yet impossible to pursue. Was Sīzǔ such a man? Was Cízàng such a man?

Wu Ye Chan Master of Fenzhou in Tang China, a native of Yongzhou in Shaanxi, did not respond to three imperial summons. Emperor Mu sent Lingzhun, the Chief Registrar of the Left Street, to carry an edict to recruit him.
The Master smiled and said, "What virtue do I, this poor monk, possess to trouble the Sovereign so repeatedly? You may go on ahead; I—"
He immediately departed. Upon arriving, he bathed, prepared his seat, and addressed his disciples, saying: "The nature of your seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing is co-eternal with the great void.
All objective realms are fundamentally empty and quiescent from the beginning. Those who are deluded do not understand this and are thus confused by objects, wandering through saṃsāra without end.
Constantly realize that all is empty; let not a single dharma confront the mind. This is the function of all Buddhas."

Having spoken these words, he sat upright and passed away at midnight. Upon reporting this to the Emperor, the Sovereign expressed great admiration and bestowed upon him the posthumous title of National Preceptor Dada (Great Realization).
Throughout the reigns of Emperors Xuanzong and Mu-tsung, the Master declined three imperial summons to attend court.
When the imperial edict arrived, Tang Lanyong did not rise.
He was a recluse at Mount Niushou in Jinling. When the Emperor heard of his reputation, he dispatched an imperial messenger to summon him for an audience.

Upon the messenger's arrival, Lanyong happened to be sitting on the ground, burning cow dung for fire; he was picking up roasted taro from the embers to eat, his cold tears flowing down to his chin. The messenger said, "The Emperor..."
The Emperor issued a decree, saying, "Venerable sir, please rise. Daorong looked at him intently without turning his head. The messenger laughed and said, "Your tears have reached your chin.

Daorong replied, "How could I have the leisure to wipe away the tears of a worldly man? When the Emperor heard this, he sighed in admiration of his extraordinary character and bestowed generous gifts upon him as a mark of honor.
Mao Si-na-seng was the monk Tang Fachong.
A native of Chengji in Longxi, at the beginning of the Zhenguan era, an imperial decree mandated the death penalty for those who privately ordained monks.
At that time, many monks were fleeing to Mount Yiyang to seek refuge, but their provisions were running short. Fachong went to the local magistrate and said: "If there should be..."

Regarding the matter of death, he personally took it upon himself; yet by providing only the provisions for the Path, he ultimately obtained blessings and protection. The Magistrate admired his resolve and, disregarding the legal prohibitions, provided him with relief.
He did not attend secular banquets.
The Tang dynasty Chan Master Taoguang built a thatched hut on the western peak of Lingyin.

When the Regional Inspector Bai Juyi prepared a meal and invited him with a poem, Taoguang replied with a verse and did not go. It contained the lines: "The city is no place for my flying staff to reach;
I fear startling the singing orioles before the painted towers. Such was the loftiness of his character.
The commentary says: There is a verse by an ancient worthy regarding declining an invitation from a high official to a banquet, which states:

"Yesterday was already past, and today is but a date; Leaving the gate leaning on my staff, I reflect once more: As a monk, one should dwell only among the mountains and valleys; To sit amidst a state official’s banquet is most inappropriate."
This is identical in spirit to the lofty aspirations of Tao Guang, following in his footsteps as if from the same mold. Alas!
These two verses should be recited by monastics morning and evening before they are truly mastered.

Fushouyi (posthumously titled Quanfu) of the Later Tang was a native of Kunshan in Wu Commandery. Having encountered Chan Master Yong of Nanta, he attained sudden enlightenment regarding the mind-ground. Later, he resided at Qinghua Chan Monastery.
When the Prince Zhongxian of the Qian family dispatched an envoy to present him with a purple *kāṣāya*, Fu submitted a memorial to decline it, and the envoy [returned].
He went again, and once more declined, saying, "It is not that I am feigning humility; I fear that later generations might emulate me and give rein to their desires.
Subsequently, he was granted the title of Chan Master Chunyi (Pure Unity), but he again firmly declined and would not accept it.

Hengchao of the Five Dynasties declined the conferment of the purple robe with firm resolve. A native of Fanyang, he resided at Kaiyuan Temple. For over twenty years, he lectured on the sutras and śāstras.

Whenever governors, prefects, or officials sent their calling cards requesting an audience, he would have his young attendant collect them; he rarely received or conversed with them in person. At that time, the commandery...
Governor Li wished to memorialize the Emperor to grant him purple robes, but Chao declined with a poem containing the lines: "I vow to transmit the sutras and treatises even unto death;

I shall not be stained by profit or fame in this life. Although Governor Li again sent messengers to urge him, Chao remained firm and unyielding, saying, "If you come again, I shall be beyond the Lulong Pass.
When Feng Gong, the Marquis of Ying and Minister of State, heard of his reputation, he composed a letter for him.
When they established friendly relations, Chao said, "I, a poor monk, abandoned my parents early to fulfill my vow of cultivation. My original aspiration was to seek renown before Maitreya;
I did not expect such rumors to spread regarding me as a minister. How could I allow my mind to dwell on empty reputation or fleeting profit? Feng Gong held him in even greater esteem.

He reported this to the court, and was granted the purple robe by imperial decree. On the day of his death, celestial music filled the sky; this was clear evidence that he had been reborn in Tuṣita Heaven.
The eulogy says: To wear the girdle of gold and purple and to frequent the gates of high ministers and counselors—this is what people deeply desire, yet they fear it most.
"It cannot be so. The two gentlemen declined repeatedly and resolutely, as if they feared defiling it. Their pure integrity was so majestic that it sweeps through the ages;
it can truly cool the feverish hearts of those who scramble for advancement and awaken the drunken eyes of those obsessed with profit and fame.
He did not delight in the royal palace.
During the Zhengbian era of the Later Tang, Zhongshan native Deng Bian applied himself to his studies with great austerity, even drawing blood to transcribe the scriptures.

At that time, the Prince of Bingzhou would not tolerate monks from outside the region; Bian went out into the wilds and hid his body within an ancient tomb. When Emperor Wu went out on a hunting excursion, Bian was just emerging from the tomb when he was seen.

His banners and horsemen returned to the burial mound. The Emperor captured him and questioned him about the reason. Upon inspecting the interior of the tomb, they found grass mats, desks, inkstones, and annotated manuscripts spread out everywhere.
Thereupon, the Emperor ordered him to enter the palace to receive offerings. Empress Dowager Cao held him in deep esteem and respect.
Huiyuan petitioned the Empress, saying, "I originally valued the study of the Dharma; remaining for so long in the royal palace was like being bound by shackles. The Emperor then released him.
His freedom was such that he tucked his letter of recommendation (by Zhao) into his sleeve.

Chan Master Xuedou Xian of Song had received the Dharma from Master Zuo of Zhimen; intending to travel through the Two Zhe regions, the Academician... [Zeng]... (Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the extant portion.)
The Duke said to him, "Lingyin is a most excellent place in the world. Master Shan was an old friend of mine; I have sent a letter of recommendation for you.

Xian arrived at Lingyin and remained submerged among the masses for three years. Suddenly, Lord Zeng, while on an official mission in Western Zhejiang, went to seek out Xian, but no one at Lingyin knew of his presence.
At that time, there were over a thousand monks; the envoy’s clerk examined the bedding registers and finally found Xian. He asked about the letter previously sent.
He took the letter from his sleeve; its seal was intact as before. He said, "Your intention is earnest, sir, but a wandering monk has no worldly desires—how could I dare hope for such recommendation?
Master Zeng laughed heartily, and Shàn marveled at him for this.
The commentary states: When people today receive a letter from a high-ranking official, they treat it as if they had obtained a precious jade tablet, seeking to sell it day and night.

Have they not heard of the tradition of Xuedou? I find it strange that while Xuedou’s handling and chanting of the Chan lineage was like a flash of lightning or a clap of thunder—unyielding to the likes of Deshan and Linji—when one examines his life, it becomes clear that his character and capacity were inherently extraordinary. Thus he is explained.
A son must not fail to love himself.
Discarding books without even unrolling them—
Master Hui’an of Wuning Temple in Song, who was a fellow student of Yuantong Xiu and Tiebi, both of whom studied under Tianyi, lived in seclusion at Wu.

"It would be better to dwell alone in a desolate village or a ruined monastery for thirty years than to have Yuantong respond to the imperial summons and reside at Fayun Monastery, where his majestic brilliance shone so brightly.
Later, he sent a letter to Dao’an; An did not even open it but threw it away. When an attendant asked the reason, An said:

'At first I thought Xiu possessed a brilliant spirit, but now I know he is merely a fool. For one who has left the household life, the cemetery and the foot of trees are where one should cultivate realization.'"

The matter is like one rushing to extinguish a fire on one's head. To have built a great house at a crossroads of eight roads for no reason, to maintain hundreds of idle fellows—this is truly urinating on one’s own bed while wide awake. What more can I say in response?
The commentary states: Xiu favored those with many followers, while An favored the solitary practitioner; this is likely true regardless of the place. Yet, An did not disparage Xiu;
he merely sought to warn the world against the masses of the stubborn and deluded. Nevertheless, it may still be acceptable to support idle men.
But what can be said of those who are supported today? They are busy men! What more need be said?
Dai Shi-fen-bo (Dai Huilian) was a native of Zhangzhou.
During the Huangyou era, he was summoned for an audience at Huacheng Hall and pleased the Emperor’s mind. He was granted the title Chan Master Dajue.
Huilian maintained the Vinaya with extreme rigor; the Emperor once sent an envoy to present him with a camphor *pātra*, but Huilian burned it before the messenger.
He replied, "In my dharma, one wears robes of ruined color and eats from an earthenware bowl. This bowl is not according to the Dharma; it should have no use.
He sent [the bowl] back to the Emperor with this report. The Emperor marveled at this for a long time.
The eulogy says: Master Lian forged his alms bowl without a trace of fear; Emperor Yingzu heard the report without a hint of anger. This is what is meant by:
"Without the Master, Guangwu could not have achieved his greatness; without Guangwu, the Master could not have realized his loftiness.
Is this not indeed a magnificent event for our school?

The general discussion above recorded loyalty to the sovereign; this section chronicles those of lofty character. If being of lofty character is the standard, then is it not the case that those loyal to the sovereign are not so? This is not so;
it depends entirely upon what one maintains. When the Way fills the mountain caves yet fame reaches the imperial court, the sovereign perceives me...
"May you descend to deliver our people—is this not the primary duty of propagating the Dharma and benefiting sentient beings?
I only regret that while the Great Way has not been established, those who distort themselves to seek honor bring shame upon the sons of Śākya. Alas!

May those who act as monks truly value themselves through the Way, so that kings and great ministers may hear of monks throughout the world who delight in the Way and forget worldly power, and marvel at them."
I admire him; his loyalty was likewise great. How could loyalty necessarily consist only of presenting one's views face-to-face to offer counsel on what to adopt or reject?
It is through this that I know Nanyang [Liu Xuan] served seven successive reigns, while Wuye declined three imperial summons. Their circumstances were different, yet their Way was the same;
their loyalty was the same.
△ The Eighth Account: The Dignified Conduct of the Sixth Patriarch of the Tang Dynasty, whose transmission of the Dharma remained hidden for a long time.
When he first visited the Fifth Patriarch, he immediately awakened to his own mind. The Patriarch said, "Your spiritual capacity is exceedingly sharp."

He went to work at a grain-threshing shed and engaged in the labor of pounding rice with mortars and pestles. He bound a stone to his waist and performed diligent, arduous toil as an offering to the assembly. Later, he transmitted the robe and the Dharma.
At midnight, he departed in secret and lived incognito among hunters for sixteen years, with disheveled hair and a soiled face.

Subsequently, he was recommended by the dragon kings and devas; thus, while at the lecture hall of Master Yinzong, they happened to discuss the wind and the banner, and the fourfold assembly was struck with wonder.
Looking up [to him], he supported and assisted in the opening of the Dharma, greatly propagating the Southern School and serving as a model for ten thousand generations.
The eulogy says: The Great Master not only opened the Dharma sixteen years after [the Buddha’s passing], but his tonsure was likewise so.

In terms of nurturing his practice deeply and accumulating its merit to such a profound degree, he is peerless throughout ancient and modern times. Is it not fitting that he serves as a model for ten thousand generations?

For ten years, Tang Guichen—originally from Changshan—kept this secret and valued it. He first studied the Vinaya, later sought out the Southern School, and traveled extensively to consult various masters of enlightenment until he attained the essential meaning.

Regarding Master Xuansha, his secret practice was submerged like a hidden pearl. At the request of the Magistrate Wang of Zhangzhou, he resided at the West Stone Lotus Palace in the city of Min for over ten years.
He kept the wondrous Way profoundly secret; only when someone approached him with earnest resolve did he expound it for them.
Subsequently, he moved to the Luohan Monastery, where he remained unperturbed amidst broken walls and dilapidated bedding. The Grand Guardian of Qinzhou...
He was requested to proclaim the Dharma. Unable to decline, he finally accepted the invitation and opened wide the gate of the Dharma. His disciples were beyond counting;
thus, he brought forth the single school of the Fa-yen lineage.
Yīngyì (fl. late Tang dynasty), Shànjìng:
A native of Jīnchéng in Cháng'ān. He traveled south to Lèpǔ, where he met Ān Gōng’s dharma heir and thereby integrated the essentials of the mind.
Later, he returned to his hometown; when the Regional Inspector Wáng established the Yǒng'ān Monastery for him to reside in, he once bathed, and śarīra appeared.
It fell down, whereupon he immediately withdrew it into secrecy and did not permit his disciples to show it to others.

Furthermore, while he was in meditative stillness, a white crane suddenly appeared, behaving with such familiarity in the courtyard as if it were listening to the Dharma; he quietly ordered someone to drive it away. All such extraordinary signs occurred, yet he never proclaimed them.

The commentary says: In ancient times, those who attained spiritual wonders kept them secret and did not proclaim them; in the present day, those who possess no spiritual wonders falsely claim such things to delude the masses.
Their hearts and deeds differ as much as heaven and earth. The wise become ever wiser, and the foolish become ever more foolish—what is there to wonder at?
Tang Puyuan mingled with woodcutters and herdsmen.
A native of Xinzheng in Zhengzhou, he received his training under Chan Master Dahui of Mount Daowei and attained the Dharma from the Great Master Ma of Jiangxi.
He concealed his brilliance and shrouded his radiance, appearing as if unable to speak. In the tenth year of the Zhenyuan era, he hung up his monk’s staff [to settle there].

At Nanquan Mountain in Chiyang, he lived among the woodcutters and herdsmen, wearing a raincoat and straw hat while feeding oxen. He cleared mountain land for slash-and-burn fields, his feet never leaving Nanquan for thirty years.
During the Taihe era, the Governor of Chiyang and the Imperial Commissioner Lu Gong and General Liu Gong earnestly requested that he open a Dharma center.
His spiritual transformation spread widely, and he was hailed as the "Ancient Buddha of Nanquan."
The commentary states: "The distant patriarch Huiyuan did not step out from Mount Lu for forty years; Master Nanquan Puyuan did not set foot beyond Nanquan for thirty years.
These were the magnificent paragons of conduct among the ancients. Yet both were matters for those who had already attained the Way; they were not appropriate for beginners.
When a monastic has not yet clarified the Great Matter, they travel thousands of miles to seek out a spiritual teacher—how could this have been the time for such [reclusion]?"
Is this not to remain stubbornly in ignorance, sitting idly and losing the opportunity for wholesome benefit? Zhaozhou traveled on pilgrimage until he was eighty;
Xuefeng ascended Mount Touzi three times and went up to Dongshan nine times. I venture to address those who would hide themselves in folly: [do not be like them].

These matters all arose from the Song dynasty Chan Master Shendǐng Yīn. A native of Yùzhōu, he was renowned as an equal to Fényáng. Before reaching full maturity, he lived in seclusion at Nányuè for twenty years before being appointed as abbot;
it was another twenty years before he finally ascended the hall to preach the Dharma. Yet all of these...
Circumstances arose from others; it was truly not his own intention.
For years he remained shut in his room.
Master Chan Shi Songyun Gai retired to the West Hall in the sixth year of the Yuanyou era. He lived in seclusion with his doors closed for three years.
Ten years. Mingwuencong Chan Master,
who had long resided in the deep mountains,
entered Mount Guangzhou alone after his great enlightenment and remained there for six years at Lu'an.
He stayed in the deep mountains of Zhōu for six years. He then went to Kuāngzhōu and remained there for another three years.
Thus, he spent a total of seventeen years practicing alone in the mountains, both walking and sitting. Only after this did he emerge into the world.
The commentary says: To walk alone and sit alone after attaining great enlightenment is indeed the intent behind Nanquan’s practice of seclusion.

Yet, for one whose initial resolve has not yet reached awakening to loathe the monastic community, fear the assembly, distance themselves from their teachers, and dwell in solitary obscurity—is this not a grave error?

He was invited eight times not to go to Song, by the Chan Master Wude of Fenyang. Although he had met seventy virtuous teachers, he did not appear in the world despite these eight successive invitations.
He lived in seclusion at Baima Temple in Xiangyang; more than a thousand monastics and laypeople from Bingzhou and Fenzhou continued to entreat him with great persistence.

Thus, he complied with the aspirations of the people. Once he arrived, the lineage’s teaching flourished greatly; yet his physical traces never crossed the threshold of the gate. He himself composed a "Song of Not Leaving the Monastery" to manifest his resolve. The eulogy says:

"Observing all the great elders of the past, after they had attained the Dharma, they for the most part concealed their brilliance and erased their splendor; only when the time was ripe did they emerge."

Although this was made manifest, the Master declined eight invitations; his profound secrecy was even more extreme. That later the school’s teaching flourished greatly—was this not because its source was deep and its stream long?
Today, young men burdened with a single talent are anxious that they will not be the first to leave the mundane world.

This too is mistaken. Even if one were to pluck them while they are still on the tree, they would ultimately lack fragrance. It behooves the patch-robed monks to use this as a constant warning to themselves.
Recorded by Fayan Yishan Yuanfawen.
He left home at the age of seven and subsequently studied the *Lotus Sūtra*, the *Prajñāpāramitā*, *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, and *Hetuvidyā* under Master Wen.
Regarding the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, Lord Wen remarked, "I have heard that the task is weighty and the path is long; I entrust you with the responsibility of propagating it.
Upon hearing this, [Wuzhuo] burned his flesh, cauterized his fingers, and drew blood to transcribe the scriptures in order to manifest his reverence for the Dharma.

He subsequently retired to Mount Wutai, where he did not cross its threshold for six years. There, he read the five thousand scrolls of the Tripitaka three times. The Imperial Preceptor sighed in admiration, saying, "In the land of Han..."
Thus it was that this monk appeared. Shortly thereafter, by the command of Prince Anxi, he opened a lecture hall at Yishan Temple. When the Son of Heaven heard of him, he summoned him to the capital;
by imperial decree, he resided at Daoyuan Jiaosi Temple and was granted a first-grade silver seal. Those seeking the precepts all received them from him.
On the twenty-fourth day of the third month in the fourth year of the Yan’yu era, he passed away while seated in meditation.
Yinyu Yuan was a native of Xian County, Quzhou. He successively studied under various great masters, including Bunan, Duanya, and Zhongfeng.
Later, he received the Dharma from Zhiyan and returned to an abandoned temple on Mount Wushi in Xian County, where he built a thatched hut to dwell in seclusion.

He did not emerge from the mountains for six years, yet his reputation reached the imperial court. A high-ranking official was dispatched to bestow upon him fragrant incense and a golden-embroidered Dharma robe, and he was granted the honorary title "Hongbian.
During the Zhizheng era, five new monasteries were established at Longmian, Guwang, and other locations;

General Discussion:

Someone asks, "When the World-Honored One first attained perfect enlightenment, he immediately expounded the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*. Yet there was a novice monk who preached this sutra at the mere age of seven.
If one insists that [the Buddha] must have remained in seclusion for many years, what would become of sentient beings? It seems we do not understand the gravity and deliberation of the ancients."
It was not merely that he excelled at forgetting the world. His Way was lofty, yet his resolve grew ever more diligent; his mind was clear, yet his conduct became increasingly cautious.

By the waters and beneath the forests, he nurtured the sacred embryo, awaiting the ripening of the fruit and the wafting of its fragrance, until the dragons and devas emerged him from concealment to lift him up and establish him in the world.
He appears to have ample leisure. You observe the Tathāgata’s benefit for sentient beings throughout his lifetime, yet you do not know of his cultivation over three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*.
Furthermore, how could you know that a seven-year-old śrāmaṇera is not one who has practiced through many lifetimes? The Buddha-dharma is not like fresh fish that must be feared of rotting away.
Though these words are small, they can serve as a metaphor for the great.
△ The Ninth Practice of Austerity:

The Venerable Mahākāśyapa, a senior *dhūta* practitioner of the Buddha’s era, was dedicated exclusively to the *dhūta* observances; even in his old age, he did not abandon them. The Buddha took pity on him for his advanced years and infirmity.
The Buddha said, "You have long endured toil and hardship; you should now take some rest. Kāśyapa continued his ascetic practices as before.
The Buddha sighed with great admiration and said, "You are able to serve as a refuge for all sentient beings; this is no different from my being in the world myself."
"If there were those who practice the dhūta austerities as you do, my Dharma would endure; otherwise, my Dharma would perish.
You are truly one who shoulders the great Dharma. Later, he transmitted the Dharma and became the First Patriarch in India.

The commentary states: The preservation or extinction of the *dhūta* practices depends upon the survival or decline of the Dharma. The Buddha’s golden mouth proclaimed this, and his words still ring in our ears.
Yet today, the monastics indulge in rich food, adorn their robes, beautify their dwellings, let their limbs grow idle, and decorate themselves with trinkets;
they act like princes and dukes without feeling shame. As the Dharma of the Final Age is about to sink, it is truly a matter for which one must wring one's hands. Kāśyapa was the patriarchal founder.
That what has been done in the two directions of the East and West is thus—could this not be because they foresaw future calamities and bequeathed their plans to their descendants?
You should follow the practices established by your ancestors; you practitioners must not abandon yourselves on account of the Dharma-ending age.

Having experienced many perils and hardships, Tanwujie of the Jin dynasty heard that Faxian and others had personally traveled to the Buddha-land. He was moved by deep emotion and made a vow to sacrifice his life;
in the first year of the Yongchu era, he gathered twenty-five like-minded companions, including Tanlang and Sengmeng, and set out from Chang’an toward the west.
He crossed the shifting sands. Above, no birds flew; below, no beasts roamed. Looking out in all directions, the vast expanse was boundless, and he knew not where he was going.
He could only rely on the sun’s position to determine east and west, and observe human bones to mark his path. Upon reaching Mount Si, the peaks were covered in perpetual snow.
Malevolent dragons spat forth venom, and winds rained down grit and pebbles. Having previously crossed the Snow Mountains, he now reached a great river flowing beneath them.

It was as swift as an arrow. A bridge was constructed by fastening ropes between the flanks of two mountains, east and west; ten people crossed at once, and once they had reached the opposite shore, they raised smoke as a signal.
When those behind saw the smoke, they knew the preceding party had already crossed and could then advance further.

If no smoke was seen for a long time, they knew that a violent wind had blown the ropes away and the people had fallen into the river. They then crossed the Great Snow Mountains, where there were precipitous cliffs and sheer walls.
He stood where there was no place to rest his feet; on the wall were old holes for wooden pegs, positioned opposite one another at regular intervals.
Holding four of these pegs, he first pulled out the lower one and then grasped the upper one, climbing from one to the next until, after three days, he finally reached level ground.
He inspected his companions and found that twelve men had perished. Continuing toward Central India, as the road was vast and desolate, he carried nothing but rock honey as provisions.
Provisions. Among the thirteen people, eight more died. Although Wujie repeatedly encountered perilous and thorny situations, he never for a moment ceased to fix his mind on Avalokiteśvara.
Upon reaching the kingdom of Śrāvastī, he encountered a herd of wicked elephants; he then took refuge in Avalokiteśvara, and suddenly a lion appeared, whereupon the elephants fled in terror.
Reaching the Ganges River, he again encountered a herd of rhinoceroses; he took refuge as before, and immediately there was a great...
Vultures flew down; even the cattle were startled and scattered. Later, he traveled by ship from South India to Guangzhou and returned carrying the scriptures.
The eulogy states: "Reading the *Record of the Western Regions*, one may still shed tears a thousand years later; as for every single word and phrase of it today..."
All [these works] are the sweat and blood of former sages. Yet some encounter them with a frivolous mind, handle them with defiled hands, or place them in unclean locations.
Others preserve them but do not read them; they read them but do not practice them;
or they employ them merely for the sake of food, clothing, wealth, profit, and fame. How tragic!
Regarding the "Dharma-Extinction Mourning Robe" (Famie shuaidie):

When Sui Lingyu saw that the teachings were being suppressed by the Northern Zhou dynasty, his grief was unbearable. He donned the *zhanshuai* (unhemmed mourning) robe and bound his head with a hempen band, as if he had lost his parents.
While leading his companions to discuss the True Principle at night, he read secular books during the day, concealing his form like withered ashes.
Zhizhen of Sui was a native of Dali in Zhaozhou.

He specialized in the cultivation of meditative observation (*guan*). Whenever deluded thoughts suddenly arose, he could not restrain them. To wait for the restoration of the Dharma, he pricked his thigh to discipline his mind.

He immediately pricked his thigh until it bled. At other times, he would embrace stones to circumambulate the stupa, never wavering for even a moment. The spots where he had pierced his thigh were mottled like brocade.
Thus he went to Western India to fetch the scriptures.
The Dharma Master Xuanzang of the Tang dynasty made a vow to seek out the scriptures. In the third year of the Zhenguan era, he traveled west alone.
Having crossed the shifting sands and passed through Gaochang, he reached Jibin. There were many tigers and leopards, and he was unable to proceed further.

Not knowing what stratagem to employ, Xuanzang closed his door and sat down. When evening came, he opened the door, and an old monk arrived. Xuanzang immediately paid him homage; the monk instructed him to recite the *Prajñāpāramitā*.

If he had followed his heart’s desire, tigers and leopards would have hidden their forms and malevolent spirits would have fled their tracks; he would have proceeded straight to the Buddha-land to retrieve the scriptures and return home.
In total, he passed through more than one hundred and fifty kingdoms before finally arriving at the capital in the winter of the nineteenth year of the Zhenguan era.

He purified his body and mind and diligently attended to all communal affairs. He provided for several hundred monks, ensuring that two meals were always prepared. Six...

He resided at Papaya Temple on Mount Wutai, living alone like a solitary shadow.

Why, then, do you now regard the journey as a toil? What is meant by the saying, "A single phrase follows another's words, and the patch-robed monks run through a thousand mountains," refers precisely to this.
Nowadays, when one is made to seek teachers and inquire after the Way, one frowns at every half-step, chasing only after profit.
If one pursues fame, one may travel lightly ten thousand *li* away, passing through eighty districts and a hundred villages; how remote such lofty conduct is—it can no longer be seen.
[Yet here,] he personally engages in manual labor.

Song Muzhe was a native of Linchuan. He styled himself Attendant Zhe and resided at Daguang Temple, where his assembly numbered two thousand. After the midday meal, he invariably held tea for the entire community.
Whenever the formal session concluded, he would personally engage in manual labor;

his attendants stood by his side as if they were strangers. At night, he would inspect the lamps in the main hall and its corridors. When weary, he would simply drape his monastic robe over his head and doze in the Three Sages Hall.

Humble himself and subjecting his person to hardship, the monk Sengzang would pay obeisance whenever he encountered a benevolent shrine and offer reverence whenever he met a man of great virtue. Whether among monks or laypeople, he would prostrate himself and run forward with bowed head and clasped hands.
In managing communal affairs, he humbled himself like a servant or slave. Upon seeing someone's old clothes, he would secretly wash and launder them. Or...
He engaged in sewing until the heat of midsummer night, when he stripped off his clothes and entered the thickets;

there, mosquitoes, gnats, horseflies, and leeches bit and sucked him until he bled, yet he constantly recited the name of Amitābha Buddha—a feat that even those skilled in calculation could not enumerate.

The commentary states: Wēnlíng has said, "To labor with a toiling body while sitting at ease to eat, or to bow the waist in ritual salutation while standing stiffly to receive [offerings]—if these do not stem from the virtue of benefiting oneself, the harm is no small matter. This Elder is surely exempt from such faults.
Regarding the diligent service of the community:
When Song Yun first visited Master Jian of Chan Temple, he conversed with him for three days and was greatly struck by his extraordinary qualities.

However, he cautioned him, instructing him to serve the community with diligent austerity. Thereupon, Yun personally attended to the well and the mortar, managed the firewood and the cooking, and oversaw all temple affairs without neglecting his duties.
When comparing the ancients with the present, none among the multitude have understood this. Master Song Yuanzhao Ben did not shrink from the toil of practice;
his teacher was Master Sheng of Yong’an. Sheng’s reputation for the Way was so weighty within the monastic community that those who returned to him were as numerous as [the clouds].
Yunben wore tattered clothes and had a soiled face; she managed the well and mortar and handled the cooking to provide for the community. At night, she would enter the room to study the Way.

Daosheng said, "The *dhūta* practice of supporting the assembly is truly arduous; are you not weary? Yunben replied, "If one were to abandon even a single dharma, one could not be said to have fulfilled *bodhi*.
If I must personally realize it in this very life, how could I dare speak of weariness?"

The commentary says: One may manage communal affairs without hindering the deliberation of ancient and modern matters; one may oversee cooking and hearthwork without obstructing entry into the chamber to study the Way.
Yet nowadays, some śramaṇas fold their hands while receiving offerings, claiming, "I am one who cultivates the Way; that person is merely one who performs worldly tasks. This is a grave error.
How different this is from antiquity!
Liu Song Daofa was a native of Dunhuang who specialized in the practice of dhyāna. Later, while traveling to Chengdu, he encountered Wang Xiuzhi and Fei Jianzhi.

He requested the masters to promote the two lands of Xingle and Xiangji. He possessed a method for instructing the assembly: he constantly practiced *piṇḍapāta* (alms-gathering), never accepting special invitations, nor participating in communal monastic meals.
Of whatever was obtained through begging, he would give a portion to insects and birds. At night, he would strip off his robes and sit in the open air to feed the mosquitoes and gadflies.
Later, while in meditative concentration (*samādhi*), he saw Maitreya Buddha emit light from his navel, which illuminated the retributions of the three miserable realms. At that time—
He intensified his diligent practice, remaining constantly seated and never lying down. In the second year of the Yuánhuí era, he passed away while in meditative absorption.
Regarding the transmission of admonitions among sage-kings, it is said: "Do not be indolent. Regarding the mutual exhortations of the Buddha’s followers, it is said: "Be careful not to be heedless."
Therefore, those who seek the Dharma forget their own bodies for the sake of the Dharma; those who benefit the multitude forget themselves for the sake of the multitude.

Yet today, young men do not even wet their ten fingers, nor do they concern themselves with a hundred tasks. When asked to hold an alms bowl, they say their arms ache; when asked to hold a broom, they say their backs hurt.
If they are urged to practice diligently day and night, they say, "My body is weak and prone to illness. Should they be further questioned, they again claim it is because they are dull-witted.
The former applies effort to wisdom; the latter applies the mind to wisdom. The fool cultivates merit; the wise cultivate wisdom. Alas!

If one speaks according to these results, it would follow that not only was Kāśyapa foolish for his ascetic practices (dhūta), and the Sixth Patriarch foolish for his work at the millstone, but that even the Buddha must have been foolish for not abandoning the merit of threading a needle. Alas!

Sincerity Moving the Precepts.
Daojin of Jin, a native of Zhangye, went to Vinaya Master Dharmakṣema to request the reception of the Bodhisattva precepts. Dharmakṣema did not grant his request.
He was instructed to perform repentance for seven days. When he went again after completing the repentance, the Master was again greatly enraged and would not allow him to enter.
He withdrew and practiced sincere worship and repentance for three years. One night, he dreamed that Śākyamuni Buddha personally conferred the precepts upon him.

The next morning, when he went to see Dharmakṣema and wished to speak of his dream, Dharmakṣema greeted him from afar, saying, "You have already received the precepts. From then on, both monastics and laypeople followed him to receive the precepts.
There were over a thousand people.
After performing repentance, Faqiao of Jin obtained a wondrous voice.
In his youth, he delighted in reciting scriptures but lacked a clear tone; thereupon, he abstained from grain and performed repentance for seven days.
Qi bowed his head to Avalokiteśvara, seeking an immediate response. His fellow students earnestly admonished him against it, but he would not listen.
On the seventh day, he felt a sudden opening within his throat; he asked for water to drink. From then on, the sound of the sutras reached as far as the neighboring village.

At the Lion Throne (Śīṃhāsana), Zhu Daosheng of the Liu Song dynasty debated the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, asserting that even those with the icchantika nature would all attain Buddhahood. The senior Dharma masters regarded this as heterodox teaching and ostracized him.
Daosheng vowed: "If what I have said does not accord with the meaning of the sūtra, I pray that my present body may suffer misfortune."
Huida replied, "Truly, this accords with the Buddha-mind. I vow that at the time of my passing, I shall occupy the lion’s seat.

He then went to Mount Huqiu in Wu Commandery, where he erected a stone as his disciple and lectured on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*. When he reached the passage concerning the existence of Buddha-nature in icchantikas, he said, "As I have explained it..."

He asked whether they accorded with the Buddha’s mind, and the stones all nodded their heads. Shortly thereafter, the "Parinirvāṇa" chapter arrived; as expected, it declared that even icchantikas possess Buddha-nature.
Later, at Mount Lu, he had just finished lecturing on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* when the assembly suddenly saw his fly-whisk fall to the ground, and he passed away while sitting upright.
The commentary states: Among the words of the Sages, there are those where the phrasing is incomplete while the meaning is perfect;

the discussion on *icchantikas* in the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* is a prime example. Why wait for the arrival of later chapters? For those who have attained the Way grasp the underlying principle, whereas those of narrow understanding cling to the literal text.

This is not limited to the case of the *icchantika* alone; rather, when one gives rise to right view, it remains unshakable, as firm as metal or stone, and one does not deviate from it even unto death.
A vow that shines brilliantly through antiquity and the present—how magnificent!

I did not dare to neglect the *poṣadha* or recklessly expound the doctrine; instead, I immediately used a blade to cut my own body, the agonizing pain of which was difficult to endure.
Consequently, I was supported back to the monastery, where for ten years I practiced sincere repentance and observed the *poṣadha* with utmost devotion and according to the prescribed ritual.
On the day of his death, a rare fragrance came to welcome him as he passed away with joy. At that time, everyone praised him for having reformed himself before his passing.
The eulogy says:
"In these times, people still value the sutras and śāstras while disregarding the precepts; for two thousand years, there has been no recitation of the precepts during the fortnightly assemblies."
Furthermore, there are those who uphold the practice. I, unassuming as I am, have revived what had fallen into ruin within the mountains; yet people still do not believe it.
The retribution is manifestly clear, as evidenced by Master Yun. I pray that those who read this will reflect upon it.
Sengyuan of the Qi dynasty recovered from leprosy.

He resided at Xue Temple in Liangzhou and did not cultivate refined conduct, drinking and eating according to his whims. Suddenly, he dreamed of a divine being who scolded him with bared teeth, saying:
"You are one who has left the household life; yet you commit such evils. Why do you not take a mirror and look at yourself? At dawn, [he awoke].
When he was by the water, he saw a dark, smudged area around his eyes and, thinking it was dirt, reached up to wipe it away. His eyebrows fell off as soon as his hand touched them.

He then reproached himself and, in deep remorse, resolved to change his habitual ways. Wearing tattered clothes and broken sandals, he maintained a single meal and a lifelong fast. From dusk until dawn, he practiced repentance with tears flowing profusely.
After more than a month, he dreamed that the deity from before smiled and said to him, "Since you recognize your faults and are able to reform, you may [proceed]."
The wise man said, "I shall now pardon you. Startled and joyful, he woke up; sweat covered his entire body, his face was moist with perspiration, and his eyebrows grew back.
Having experienced the retribution for two lifetimes, he knew with certainty that the three periods of time are not in vain.
Thereafter, he served the Dharma with utmost sincerity without ever falling away, and eventually became a renowned monk.
Qinku Fajie Liangdao Chao was a native of Wu Commandery. Seeing that Dharma Master Min’s learning and understanding were preeminent within the realm, he desired to emulate him.

He suspended his sleep and forgot the taste of food, continuing his studies from night until day. In a dream, someone said to him: "Dharma Master Min, during the time of Vipaśyin Buddha, had already..."

"You are able to lecture and explain. You have only just begun your cultivation; how could you possibly be his equal? Simply apply yourself with diligence, and do not worry that you will not attain understanding according to your own capacity.
Thereupon, he applied himself with tireless effort until, after some time, he attained profound and thorough penetration.
The Dharma Master Liang Chong was thirty-eight years old when he encountered the Daoist practitioner Fayuan, who said to him, "When you reach forty years of age, you shall die;
there is no way to avoid it. Only by praying with utmost sincerity to the Buddhas and repenting for your past transgressions might you have hope."
Chong led him before a mirror to examine it; there was a dark vapor upon his face. Thereupon, he sold his robes and bowl to purchase incense and offerings.

He traveled east to Guangxing Temple in Haiyan, where he closed the doors to perform rites of repentance, cutting off all worldly affairs. During the day he forgot to eat or rest; at night he did not even remove his robes.
When he reached the age of forty, on the evening of the last day of the year, he suddenly felt swelling and pain in both ears. That night, he performed his repentance rites until the fourth watch.

He heard a voice outside the door saying, "Your karmic debt for death has already been exhausted. He hurriedly opened the door, but saw nothing at all. By the following morning, the black vapor had vanished, and bone had grown back in both ears.
He maintained a regular practice of limiting himself to one hundred prostrations before the Buddha each day; later, when he fell ill, he could not [complete them].
He was able to rise again. Just as on his bed, he would bow and look up with reverent devotion a hundred times at each appointed hour. He passed away at the age of seventy-four;
by reciting the sutras, he had extended his lifespan.

Zhicang of the Liang dynasty was a native of Wu Commandery. He resided at Kaishan Temple on Mount Zhong. Upon meeting a physiognomist, the man told him, "Dharma Master, your intelligence surpasses that of all men;
however, it is a pity that your life will not be long—you shall live for only thirty-one years. At that time, Zhicang was twenty-nine years old.

Thereupon, he ceased his lectures and delved into the scriptural treasury. There he obtained the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, which he recited with utmost sincerity, prostrating before the Buddha and performing repentance day and night without ceasing.

He ceased [the recitation]. When the appointed time arrived, he suddenly heard a voice from the air saying, "Your lifespan was originally exhausted; by the power of the merit of Prajñā, you have been granted double that span.

Later, when he encountered the person who had previously predicted his death, he was struck with wonder and unable to fathom it. He recounted the circumstances to Cáng, who first realized that the power of the scripture is inconceivable.

The commentary says: Longevity and brevity of life are matters of destiny (*bhāga*). If one could extend their lifespan through ritual repentance and the recitation of sutras, then the doctrine of past causes (*pūrvahetu*) would be discarded.
Alas! By returning his belt, the signs of an early death were removed; by rescuing ants from drowning, the form of nobility was manifested.

Human effort can still turn back the tide of untimely death, let alone the inconceivable power of the Triple Gem. My only regret is that my own sincerity cannot equal that of those two gentlemen. [He] beat the drum and blew the flute.
Thus, they took the *sūtras* as their texts and used the crossed pestle and mortar to perform their rites; how then can one wonder that there is no means for spiritual resonance?

To repay this kindness, you may offer ten rolls of silk. The wife offered the silk, which Xing distributed among the assembly. When the assembly asked why he had struck the bell, [he explained].
