Then he struck it three times. Upon striking it for a long duration, he prayed again: 'May those in the various evil realms who hear the sound of my bell all be freed from suffering and affliction.
In the bitter cold of midwinter, when the skin cracks and the flesh chafes, and blood congeals within the palms, one must not shrink from such toil."

The Vinaya Master Daoxuan of the Tang dynasty was protected by celestial deities. His surname was Qian. Initially, after listening to the Vinaya from his teacher only once, he wished to travel abroad to study;

however, his teacher rebuked him, saying, "One should go far starting from what is near, and there is a proper time for cultivation and renunciation. Thus, he was compelled to listen to it ten times. Subsequently, he maintained the Vinaya with rigorous discipline.
It was a rare occurrence in this world. While practicing the Way on a mountain during the middle watch of the night, he stumbled and fell against a stone step.
A heavenly deity clad in armor supported him from the side. Xuan asked, "What deity are you? He replied, "I am Zhang Qiong, the son of King Vaicravana.

Because your teacher’s precepts and virtue are lofty and sublime, I have come to provide protection. Xuan then questioned him extensively regarding the Buddha’s era, receiving detailed answers for every point. Finally, [the deity] bestowed the Buddha’s teachings upon Xuan.
A tooth relic was presented as a token of faith. He was titled the Master of the Southern Mountain, Vinaya Master Chengzhao. The eulogy states:
"The Vinaya is not a matter of profound metaphysics, and Master Xuanchang was no dull-witted person; why then did he linger for ten hearings?

It was truly because the precepts are the foundation of the Way, and he desired them to permeate the skin and marrow so that they would remain firm and unchanging. As for those who receive the precepts today..."

Once having received [the teachings], they place them high on a shelf; they are not even able to roughly investigate their meaning, let alone a master lecturing ten times and a disciple listening ten times.
Thus I know that Master Xuan’s teacher was no ordinary man, and that there has long been a tradition of great sages emerging from his school.
"An Account of the Pure Land by Huiri of the Tang Dynasty: Setting sail across the sea, he reached India to visit learned masters and inquire about the essential methods of the shortcut path.
The scholars of India all praised the Pure Land. Upon reaching a great mountain to the northeast of the kingdom of Gandhāra, he encountered Avalokiteśvara."
He prostrated himself before the image for seven days and nights, further abstaining from food, vowing to end his life if his purpose were not fulfilled.

On the night of the seventh day, he suddenly beheld Avalokiteśvara manifesting a body of purple-gold, seated upon a precious lotus flower. The Bodhisattva extended his hand to touch the practitioner’s head and said:

"If you wish to transmit the Dharma to benefit yourself and others, you must contemplate Amitābha Buddha in the Western World of Ultimate Bliss; you should know that this is the Dharma of the Pure Land."

The Gate of Supreme Excellence surpasses all conditioned phenomena. Having finished speaking, it suddenly vanished. Returning to Chang’an, [Daoxuan] universally exhorted others to practice mindfulness of the Buddha. He praised this, saying:
"The response of Kāñcanamālā to Avalokiteśvara and the response of the Bamboo Grove to Mañjuśrī are largely similar;

in both cases, the response occurred because of the utmost sincerity. There is no room for doubt. Instances of such responses in the Pure Land are not limited to a single person; they are detailed and fully recorded in previous accounts."
This has been discussed in the section on "Birth" (*jìngzhōng*) and need not be elaborated upon here.
Regarding the Chan Master Yongming Yanshou of the Wuyue period, who was once a granary clerk: he used official funds to release living beings and consequently faced the death penalty. Wuyue...
The King released him, and he left the household life to become a monk. He once performed the *Lotus Sūtra* repentance ritual for twenty-one days with the utmost sincerity and devotion.
In a dream, he saw Avalokiteśvara pouring nectar into his mouth; consequently, he attained unimpeded eloquence.

Tán Róng of the Táng dynasty practiced repentance and received a prediction of enlightenment. During the spring and summer he expounded the teachings; during the autumn and winter he sat in meditation. When the Regional Inspector presented him with three grains of *śarīra*, he vowed to obtain them all.
He subsequently acquired four hundred grains of *śarīra*. He performed the Vaipulya repentance ritual together with the temple monk Sēng Dìng.
Within the radiance, he saw the seven Buddhas all appearing. One Buddha looked back at Rong and said, "I am Śākyamuni.
Because your physical vessel is pure, I have come to bestow upon you this prediction: in the future, you shall become a Buddha named Puming (Universally Peaceful). That winter, Rong passed away.
A rare fragrance permeated the room.
From his mouth issued the scent of blue lotuses.

Tang Sui-duan then resided at De-run Temple, where he devoted himself single-mindedly to the Lotus Sūtra, reciting it constantly throughout the twelve periods of the day without ceasing until he grew old.

His devotion grew ever more profound. In the second year of the Xuántóng era, he suddenly passed away while sitting in the lotus posture. In an instant, seven stalks of blue lotuses emerged from his mouth.
He was buried at the foot of the eastern mountain, where his tomb frequently emitted light for over twenty years. When the tomb was opened and inspected, his physical form appeared as if alive.
The community welcomed him back to the monastery, where they lacquered and clothed the remains; they now exist there, preserved in what is known as the Zhēnshēn (True Body) Hall.

In the general discussion of my recorded ancient practices, I conclude this volume with the theme of resonance and response (*ganying*). A bystander laughed and said: "The Way is without cultivation and without realization.

If there is no cultivation, then that which resonates is empty; if there is no realization, then that which responds is quiescent. To be busily preoccupied with resonance and response is itself a form of calculation."
"Is it not a mind seeking merit and profit? I replied: "When a drumstick moves the drum, it responds with sound;
when the moon moves the water, it responds with a reflection. Wherein lie 'schemes' and 'calculations'? Therefore, when a loyal minister makes his vow, sprouts emerge from withered bamboo;

when a filial son weeps, even solid ice melts. How can this principle be considered extraordinary? If there were no way for such resonance to occur, then the law of cause and effect would utterly vanish."
To be reckless and indifferent toward emptiness invites calamity and misfortune; one should surely be cautioned against this.

I know that those who settle for the lowly and mundane while hoping to attain the unsurpassed Buddha-vehicle are like one who has not yet entered a dream. Your disciple.

trembling with awe, I knew not whence it came. My mind was as if dead and my spirit lost, suddenly casting off all former steps;
